description: At Enceladus’s south pole, the ice above its hidden ocean may be only one to five kilometres thick, compared with Europa’s newly estimated 29 kilometres. But a spacecraft might not need to drill through it at all: Enceladus already blasts material from its ocean  Space DailyA moon does not need sunlight to keep its interior warm. Io is ablaze with volcanoes, Europa hides an ocean, and Enceladus leaks heat and water from its south pole into space — worlds kept active by the gravitational grip of planets that never lets go.  Space DailyEnceladus appears to have almost everything life should need — water, chemistry, hydrothermal energy and an ocean capable of lasting geological ages. If we search it thoroughly and find nothing alive, that failure may become one of astrobiology’s most imp  Space DailyThe idea that Earth is the Solar System's ultimate water world is misleading: Europa likely holds more than twice our ocean's volume beneath a crust of ice, while Enceladus is continuously venting material from its hidden ocean directly into space.  Space DailySome of the most promising places to search for alien life aren't planets at all, but moons — because Europa and Enceladus keep oceans liquid beneath their ice partly through the gravitational squeezing of giant planets, an internal heat source that doesn't car  Space Daily
